paragraphs.source_en: After a brief consultation, the matter was quickly settled: my master was actually going to submit to hypnotism. I had never seen such a thing before, and was secretly delighted, so I watched respectfully from the corner of the sitting room. The doctor first began by hypnotizing my master's eyes. His method was to stroke the eyes, repeatedly passing his hand downward over the eyelids. Although my master already had both eyes tightly shut, Dr. Amaki still kept making the same motion in the same direction as best he could. After a while, Dr. Amaki asked my master, “As I keep stroking your eyelids like this, your eyelids are gradually beginning to feel heavy, are they not?” My master said, “Yes, they do feel somewhat heavy.” Dr. Amaki went on stroking downward without stopping and said, “They are growing heavier and heavier, are they not?” My master must have felt that this was so, for he sat there without saying a word. The same rubbing procedure continued for another three or four minutes. At last Dr. Amaki said, “Now! You can no longer open your eyes.” Poor fellow! My master's eyes had gone blind at last. “I really cannot open them now?” my master asked. “No, certainly not. They will not open.” Dr. Amaki replied. My master silently kept both eyes tight shut, and I too truly believed that his eyes were done for. After a little while, Dr. Amaki said, “If you do not believe me, try opening them if you can. In any case, they absolutely will not open.” No sooner had my master said, “Is that so?” than both his eyes snapped open just as usual. My master smiled and said, “It did not work.” Dr. Amaki laughed along with him and said, “Indeed, it did not work.” The hypnotism ended in failure after all. Dr. Amaki went home as well.

paragraphs.source_en: Then came another visitor. It was extremely rare for so many people to call at my master's house. In the home of a master who has so little social intercourse, such a phenomenon was almost unbelievable. But the visitor had indeed come, and he was a rare guest. It is necessary to say a few words about this rare guest, not simply because he was rare; as I have already said, I am describing the ripples left by that great incident. And this rare guest is material that cannot be overlooked in describing those ripples. I do not know his name, but it should be enough to say that he was a man past forty, with a long face and a goatlike beard. Meitei is an aesthete; this man I intend to call a philosopher. Why do I call him a philosopher? Not because he paraded himself as Meitei does, but simply because, as I watched the manner in which he conversed with my master, I could not help feeling that he looked very much like a philosopher. It appeared that the two of them were old schoolmates, and their way of talking was extremely free and easy.
